IBKR key metrics — fee toll, franchise scale, API moat

IBKR-zbar-2026-09-21 · USD · series 2026-09-21T23:30:00Z · built 2026-09-21 19:47 UTC

The short version

Own IBKR for three to ten years. The business is a brokerage tollbooth: commissions and related fees on a growing global account base, with an API surface that still looks like the natural home for serious automated investing. The fear that price competition and agentic brokers hollow out the toll is the mispricing to watch — not a one-quarter soft print on net interest. What would change the view first is a sustained break in the fee toll (commission dollars falling while accounts keep rising, or $/order collapsing without a volume explanation). Second is clear loss of the agentic API lane — share we cannot yet measure, so design-wins and execute-native MCP posture are the live proxy. Third, and secondary, is a multi-quarter stall in the international franchise. NII and market-making stay in the archive footnote. They are not the hero.

IBKR Desk · Latent capital · pack 2026-09-21 · as of Q2’26 (period end 2026-06-30)

Interactive Brokers is not a retail meme shop waiting for zero commissions to erase it. It clears and carries trades for a large, increasingly global client base, charges a toll on that activity, and runs one of the deepest public brokerage APIs in the industry. The stock still often prices as if the toll were fragile and as if interest income were the whole story. The metrics below are the scoreboard that decides whether that fear is earned.

1. What IBKR is and how it makes money

IBKR runs a brokerage. Clients open accounts, fund them, and trade across many markets. Revenue that matters for this thesis shows up first as commissions and other fees and services — the fee toll. Net revenues and pretax income sit beside that toll as an honesty check. They are never stacked with it; they are not pieces of the same total.

In the second quarter of 2026 the company printed $673M of commissions and $87M of other fees and services, against $1,896M of net revenues and $1,456M of pretax income (~76.8% pretax margin). A year earlier commissions were $516M and other fees $62M. The toll grew. It did not thin out into a rounding error.

Together, commissions plus other fees were about 40% of net revenues that quarter. That is a mix share, not a margin claim — and it leaves room for interest and other lines without making them the story.

Inside the contract-revenue note, commissions still dominate. The Q2’26 ASC mix was commissions $673M, market data $23M, risk exposure $25M, payment for order flow $18M, FDIC sweep $10M, and other fees $11M. Commissions are roughly 89% of that disclosed fee stack. The non-commission ASC lines sum to $87M — the same dollars as the P&L “other fees and services” line this quarter.

Minimum-activity fees are not printed in this series. Do not invent an API or Lite attach rate from PFOF or FDIC sweep. Those are fee types, not product telemetry.

Net revenues $1,896M versus $1,480M a year earlier; pretax $1,456M versus $1,104M. Margin held in the mid-to-high 70s. That is the honesty panel next to the toll — parallel metrics, never a stack.

Archive footnote (not hero). Net interest income, NIM, and interest-earning balances are disclosed in MD&A and inventoried for Product, but they are not the analytics series of record for this pack. Market-making segment history is legacy and archive. They are not promoted into the fee-toll thesis, and they are not charted.

2. Growth engine vs legacy core

Think of the stack as franchise scale on one side and toll quality on the other — sharing one brokerage.

Franchise growth — accounts, DARTs, and customer equity. These answer whether the client base and its activity are still compounding.

Toll quality — commission dollars per order and per account, fee yield on equity, and the accounts-versus-intensity decomp. These answer whether the toll still collects as the franchise scales.

Globality — international share of management geo net revenues. Supportive color for the global-franchise pillar, not a substitute for the toll.

API — qualitative moat with an honest gap. Product surface is real; share metrics are null.

Accounts: 5.185M at mid-2026 versus 3.866M a year earlier (~+34%). Customer equity: $930.3B versus $664.6B (~+40%). Equity prints are sparse before 2023 in this extract — the chart uses the dense window from early 2023.

DARTs 4.824M versus 3.552M (~+36%). Commission per cleared commissionable order: $2.64 versus $2.65 a year ago, and $3.16 at the dense-series start in early 2023. That is a gentle glide in unit price while activity scaled — not a toll collapse. Activity rose; $/order stayed in the mid-$2s.

Accounts and equity are franchise. DARTs are activity. $/order is the issuer’s own intensity print. Do not stack them.

DERIVED framework — labeled FACT / DERIVED / ASSUMPTION / GAP

3. Fee-toll intensity (DERIVED)

Derived intensity at Q2’26 (both legs present):

  • Commissions per account ≈ $129.80 (versus ≈ $133.47 a year earlier)
  • Average equity per account ≈ $179k
  • DARTs per account ≈ 0.930 (versus ≈ 0.919)
  • Quarterly fee yield on client equity ≈ 7.23 bps (simple ×4 ≈ 29 bps — labeled simple, not TTM)

Commissions grew +30.4% nominal year over year and +26.1% in 2026-06 CPI dollars. The franchise got bigger in real terms, not just inflated ones.

Equity grew faster than commission dollars, so yield compressed even as the toll’s absolute dollars rose. Equity growth includes market moves — a caveat, not a beta attribution this cut.

The dollar decomp is blunt. Commissions rose +$157M year over year. Account growth contributed about +$176M; softer commissions-per-account took back about −$19M. Accounts carried the print. Intensity was a modest drag. That is an identity split, not a causal proof — but it is the right shape for a scaling franchise with a slightly easier unit take.

DARTs and accounts both co-move tightly with commissions in the dense window. House intensity print remains the issuer’s $/cleared order. Trading days are not disclosed here, so there is no desk-invented dollars-per-DART-day.

4. Globality (supportive)

Management geo P&L for Q2’26: US net revenues $1,284M, international $612M — international about 32% of the US+Intl total. Pretax: US $1,076M / Intl $380M.

That is management geography, not contract-revenue location. Near one-third international is supportive of the global franchise — not a stall print. Empty Q1 geo stubs in this extract stay blank; they are not interpolated.

Commission dollars by geography and Pro/Lite cohort splits remain null. Do not dress consolidated commissions up as a geo fee toll.

5. API moat — qualitative, share still a gap

IBKR still discloses no API clients, API DARTs, or automated-order share. The quantitative pillar is unmeasured.

What is knowable: the product surface is deep (Web API, TWS/Gateway, FIX, Excel bridges; marketing claims on the order of 170 markets / 40 countries). That supports multi-asset, global, systematic strength. It does not by itself prove “agentic defaults to IBKR.”

The clearest 2026 design-win tension is MCP posture. IBKR’s official MCP is assistive — AI drafts, human reviews and submits; FAQ language says AI integrations do not automate trading. Peers (notably Alpaca, and tastytrade more recently) market execute-native agent paths. That is pressure on a narrow “agentic prefers IBKR” claim. It is not a share-based falsification, because share is still null.

Watch for IR disclosure of any API metric, a flip of IBKR’s MCP FAQ toward unattended execute, and peer MCP adoption — not for invented attach rates from PFOF.

6. Unit economics → valuation

Valuation for this pack follows the desk hierarchy, with fee-toll intensity folded into the close — not parked in an orphan dig.

1. Toll dollars and mix — commissions / other fees / ASC stack. 2. Intensity — CPC, CPA, DARTs/account, fee yield, accounts-vs-intensity decomp. 3. Franchise scale — accounts, equity, DARTs. 4. Multiples — weekly trailing PE continuous; pe_ttm / pe_fy / forward sit beside.

Method & definitional notes
  • Intensity prints (CPA, DARTs per account, fee yield, the accounts-vs-CPA split, real commissions) are DERIVED. The issuer intensity print is commission per cleared order.
  • Quarterly fee yield ×4 is a simple annualization, not a TTM yield. Equity growth includes market moves.
  • The accounts-versus-intensity split is an identity, not a causal proof.
  • Weekly trailing PE breaks across the Alpaca hole (2019-W40 → 2020-W31) and does not smooth split weeks 2025-W25/W26. Residual Q4 net income inside TTM is labeled. Incomplete W38 is excluded.
  • pe_ttm 34.67 (price 86.745 on 2026-09-16) is a different window from weekly W37 ~36.25. Street FY1/FY2 sit beside trailing. Forward NTM stays blank.
  • API client share is unmeasured. Nothing in the fee stack is an API attach rate.
  • Net interest income and market-making are an archive footnote, not a chart.
  • Non-additive: Commissions and other fees are not slices of net revenues — do not stack C1 with C3.
  • Non-additive: Net revenues and pretax income are parallel (C3 grouped only).
  • Non-additive: Accounts, equity, DARTs, and $/order are parallel franchise and intensity metrics — never stacked.
  • Non-additive: ASC 606 fee mix is consolidated contract revenue, not management geo P&L.
